title: How Alliances Survive
gist: Campbell and Doshi argue current alliance pessimism is overstated: the U.S. alliance system has survived comparably severe historical shocks (Suez, French NATO withdrawal, the Nixon Shock, Plaza Accord), allied threat perceptions of China and Russia are converging for the first time in a generation, and powerful economic, technological, and military 'gravitational forces' — plus a quiet professional 'deep state' of alliance managers — are binding allies to Washington faster than political rhetoric is pulling them apart, positioning the alliance system to evolve into 'allied scale' capable of outweighing China.

insights.claim: Campbell and Doshi argue alliance pessimism is understandable but significantly overstated, resting on three points: the alliance system has weathered comparably serious historical shocks before; the threats that gave rise to the alliances (China and Russia) have intensified and allied threat perceptions are converging as never before; and powerful economic, technological, and military gravitational forces continue pulling allies toward Washington even as some try to de-risk.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: Establishes the article's core contrarian thesis against the dominant 'alliances are dying' media narrative, directly relevant to long-horizon positioning on transatlantic and Indo-Pacific defense-industrial cooperation.
insights.quote: First, the alliance system has weathered now forgotten shocks at least as serious as these, and the present ones owe more to presidential personality than to durable new politics. Second, the threats that gave rise to the alliances have not faded but intensified and converged... Third, powerful gravitational forces continue to pull allies together economically, technologically, and militarily

insights.claim: Allowed to harden into conventional wisdom, alliance pessimism risks becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy: if policymakers become convinced the alliances cannot be saved, they will stop doing the work needed to sustain them.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: Frames elite narrative-setting itself as a causal variable in alliance durability, relevant for assessing how think-tank and media discourse could shape actual policy outcomes independent of underlying fundamentals.
insights.quote: Allowed to harden into conventional wisdom, pessimism risks becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy, as policymakers, convinced the alliances cannot be saved, stop doing the work to ensure they endure.

themes.theme: Historical shocks the alliance system already survived

insights.claim: Even under the second Trump administration, the U.S. has not credibly threatened financial calamity against an ally the way it did to Britain during the 1950s Suez crisis, nor has an ally expelled U.S. troops as France did when it withdrew from NATO's unified command in the 1960s, nor has Congress nearly cut U.S. forces in Europe in half as the 1970s Mansfield Amendment nearly did.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: Provides three specific, dated historical benchmarks (Suez, French NATO exit, Mansfield Amendment) that current tensions have not yet matched, useful for calibrating just how severe today's alliance strain actually is in comparative terms.
insights.quote: Even under Trump, the United States has not credibly threatened financial calamity against an ally, as it did to the United Kingdom, in the 1950s, to halt its intervention in Suez. Nor has an ally expelled American troops or seriously undermined an alliance structure, as France did, in the 1960s... The United States has not withdrawn large numbers of troops from allies, as the Senate nearly forced it to do, in the 1970s

insights.claim: The Plaza Accord of 1985 forced Japan's yen to double against the dollar within three years — an adjustment far larger than the 15 percent tariff Japanese exports currently face — and Nixon's 1971 unilateral end of dollar-gold convertibility plus a 10 percent import surcharge was a more significant unilateral economic shock to allies than today's tariffs, yet the economic alliance system endured both.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: Quantifies two historical precedents (Plaza Accord's currency shock, the Nixon Shock) as larger economic disruptions to allies than the current tariff regime, directly informing how much economic damage the alliance system has already proven capable of absorbing.
insights.quote: In 1985, the Plaza Accord forced allies to make a major currency adjustment under the shadow of protectionist pressure, straining the German and Japanese economies more severely than the tariffs allies confront today; within three years, the yen doubled against the dollar, an adjustment far larger than the 15 percent tariff on Japanese exports.

insights.claim: The one genuine exception to historical precedent is Trump's threat of force against Greenland, which could collapse the alliance system if actually carried out — but the threat is so extreme and personalistic that no serious figure in either party has endorsed it; House Speaker Mike Johnson called military intervention there 'not appropriate' and Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he doesn't 'see military action being an option.'
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: Isolates Greenland as the single genuine tail-risk scenario that would break the historical-resilience pattern, while noting bipartisan Republican leadership has explicitly disavowed it — a useful marker for monitoring whether this specific red line gets crossed.
insights.quote: House Speaker Mike Johnson said that U.S. military intervention in Greenland “would not be appropriate,” and Senate Majority Leader John Thune said, “I don’t see military action being an option here.” Trump walked it back.

themes.theme: Public opinion contradicts the elite pessimism narrative

insights.claim: According to Chicago Council on Global Affairs polling dating back to 1974, the share of Americans who believe Washington should make major decisions together with allies rather than go it alone is now at a 50-year high, and the belief that maintaining existing alliances is 'very effective' rose from 32 percent in 2016 to 55 percent today, a ten-year high among both Democrats and Republicans.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the elite media narrative of collapsing American support for alliances with hard polling data showing the opposite trend at a 50-year high — a key data point for assessing the political durability of alliance-supportive policy.
insights.quote: the share of Americans who believe Washington should make major decisions together with allies rather than go it alone now stands at a 50-year high. Throughout the Trump era, from 2016 to today, the belief that maintaining existing alliances is “very effective” for advancing U.S. aims increased from 32 percent to 55 percent, reaching ten-year highs among both Democrats and Republicans.

insights.claim: European Council on Foreign Relations polling shows a clear majority in 13 of 15 European countries surveyed (and a plurality in the remaining two) believe the U.S. relationship will 'get better again' once Trump leaves office, with fewer than a third believing the damage will be permanent.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: Shows European publics themselves largely view current tensions as personalistic to Trump rather than a permanent U.S. posture shift — relevant to gauging how quickly European defense and trade policy could normalize under a future administration.
insights.quote: a clear majority of citizens in 13 of the 15 European countries polled, and a plurality in the remaining two, believe that the relationship will “get better again” once Trump leaves office. Fewer than a third believe the damage will last after he leaves office.

themes.theme: Converging threat perceptions of China and Russia

insights.claim: For the first time since the Cold War, threat perceptions of China and Russia are converging across the Atlantic and Pacific: NATO communiqués now brand China a 'decisive enabler' of Russia's war, its secretary-general argues the Indo-Pacific and European theaters must be viewed 'as one,' and NATO's four Indo-Pacific partners (Australia, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea) now regularly attend its summits.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: Documents a structural, institutional merger of the Atlantic and Pacific security theaters (shared NATO summit attendance, joint threat-labeling of China) that materially expands the potential scope of coordinated allied action against both China and Russia.
insights.quote: Reflecting that realization, NATO’s communiqués now brand China a “decisive enabler” of Russia’s war, and its secretary-general argues that the Indo-Pacific and European theaters must be viewed “as one.”... The leaders of NATO’s four Indo-Pacific partners—Australia, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea—now regularly attend its summits.

insights.claim: European leaders now speak of a second 'China shock': Macron says subsidized Chinese manufactured goods are 'literally killing a large part of European industry,' von der Leyen warns of Chinese 'overcapacities that erode our own manufacturing base' as 'simply not sustainable,' and Merz has floated a new Plaza Accord to force an appreciation of China's currency.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: Names three top European leaders explicitly framing China as the primary industrial threat, aligning European economic-security concerns with the long-standing U.S. view — a convergence relevant to forecasting coordinated Western tariff or currency action against China.
insights.quote: European leaders now speak of a second “China shock,” a flood of subsidized manufactured goods that, as Macron has put it, are “literally killing a large part of European industry.” Von der Leyen has warned of Chinese “overcapacities that erode our own manufacturing base” and calls the situation “simply not sustainable.” Merz has floated a new Plaza Accord to force an appreciation of China’s currency.

themes.theme: The gravitational forces binding allies to the U.S.

insights.claim: The United States now absorbs 20 to 30 percent of all allied exports, a much higher share than five years ago; over the last five years exports to China fell roughly 15 percent for Europe and 20 percent each for Japan, South Korea, and India, while exports to the United States rose roughly 30 percent each for Europe, South Korea, and India.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: A precise, quantified trade-reorientation data set (U.S. export share rising 30% while China exposure falls 15-20% across major allied economies) directly relevant to forecasting continued U.S.-allied trade interdependence despite political friction.
insights.quote: Last year, even amid the trade war, Europe, Japan, and India all exported significantly more to the United States than to China; over the last five years, exports to China fell roughly 15 percent for Europe, 20 percent for Japan, 20 percent for South Korea, and 20 percent for India—while exports to the United States rose roughly 30 percent each for Europe, South Korea, and India.

insights.claim: Three U.S. 'hyperscalers' — Amazon, Google, and Microsoft — account for about two-thirds of the global cloud market while European providers hold barely 15 percent of their own domestic market; U.S. hyperscalers are expected to spend more than $700 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026 against European sovereign AI spending of roughly $13 billion.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: A striking ~54x spending gap ($700B vs $13B) between U.S. hyperscaler AI infrastructure investment and European sovereign AI spending in 2026, quantifying how far behind Europe's 'AI sovereignty' push actually is and how deep transatlantic cloud/AI dependency will remain.
insights.quote: Three U.S. “hyperscalers”—Amazon, Google, and Microsoft—account for about two-thirds of the global cloud market, while European providers hold barely 15 percent of their own domestic market. U.S. hyperscalers are expected to spend more than $700 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026, against European sovereign spending of roughly $13 billion.

insights.claim: More than 80 percent of Europe's new $860 billion rearmament effort remains open to U.S. companies, and the share of European defense procurement going to U.S. companies climbed from about 28 percent in 2019-21 to 51 percent in 2022-24, as urgent post-Ukraine demand drove Europe toward the only supplier able to deliver at speed and scale.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: Shows European defense rearmament — often framed as 'de-risking' from the U.S. — has actually increased the U.S. share of European defense procurement (28% to 51% in three years), a counterintuitive but concrete data point for defense-industrial investors assessing transatlantic supply-chain exposure.
insights.quote: the share of European defense procurement going to U.S. companies climbed by one measure from about 28 percent in 2019–21 to 51 percent in 2022–24, as the urgency of the war in Ukraine brought demand that only the United States could meet at speed and scale.

themes.theme: The 'real deep state': professional alliance cooperation persists

insights.claim: Despite trade tensions, India and the United States signed a new ten-year defense framework strengthening interoperability across every domain in October 2025, even as India seethed under record U.S. tariffs — illustrating that alliance professionals keep security cooperation insulated from political trade fights.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: A specific, dated (October 2025) example of security cooperation continuing to deepen despite simultaneous trade conflict — evidence for the article's 'deep state' thesis that bureaucratic-level alliance cooperation is more resilient than headline political rhetoric.
insights.quote: Even as India seethed under the record tariffs the United States imposed, the defense relationship stayed insulated from the trade fight: in October 2025, the two countries signed a new ten-year defense framework strengthening interoperability across every domain.

insights.claim: AUKUS survived a skeptical 'America first' Pentagon review and changes of government in all three member states (Australia, the UK, and the U.S.), while the Philippines' annual Balikatan military exercise swelled in 2025 to its largest iteration ever, with 16,000 troops and Japanese forces participating.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: Two concrete data points (AUKUS surviving a hostile policy review across three governments; Balikatan reaching a record 16,000 troops in 2025) showing Indo-Pacific alliance cooperation deepening operationally even amid political noise.
insights.quote: AUKUS, subjected to a skeptical “America first” Pentagon review, emerged intact, having by then survived changes of government in all three member states. In the Philippines, the annual military exercise called Balikatan (meaning “shoulder to shoulder”) swelled in 2025 to its largest iteration ever with 16,000 troops, allied contingency plans, and Japanese forces.

themes.theme: The alternative world orders and the case for 'allied scale'

insights.claim: The most likely alternative to a renewed alliance system is not multipolarity, spheres of influence, or a great-power concert but partial Chinese preeminence, given China's twice-the-U.S. manufacturing capacity, an economy 30 percent larger by purchasing power, the world's largest navy, a $1.2 trillion global goods surplus, and a commanding lead in technologies from EVs to robotics.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: Provides a hard, quantified scale comparison (2x manufacturing, 30% larger PPP GDP, $1.2T goods surplus) establishing why China is treated as a unique, non-peer great power rather than one of several roughly-equal poles — the analytical basis for the 'allied scale' argument.
insights.quote: China has twice the United States’ manufacturing capacity, an economy 30 percent larger by purchasing power, the world’s largest navy, an unprecedented $1.2 trillion global goods surplus, and a commanding lead in technologies from electric vehicles to robotics.

insights.claim: If U.S. allies pooled markets, investment, technology, and military capability into 'allied scale,' the resulting coalition would have more than twice China's GDP adjusted for purchasing power, more than twice its military spending, the top position in active patents and top-cited publications, and half of global manufacturing to China's one-third.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: Quantifies the theoretical payoff of a pooled-allied-capacity strategy (2x China's PPP GDP and military spending, 50% vs 33% of global manufacturing) — the article's central prescriptive framework and a benchmark for tracking progress toward it.
insights.quote: Coming together in this way would produce a coalition that would have more than twice China’s GDP adjusted for purchasing power and more than twice its military spending; it would be the top producer of active patents and top-cited publications and the top trading partner of most countries in the world, and it would account for half of global manufacturing to China’s one-third.

insights.claim: Despite Trump's help, China has achieved little in its coalition-splitting strategy against allied unity, relying too heavily on coercive instruments like rare-earth threats even against Europe and Japan when a defter approach might have been more effective at pulling allies away from Washington.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: A contrarian read that China is overplaying its coercive hand (rare earths) against Europe and Japan, potentially accelerating rather than preventing the very allied convergence Beijing fears — worth monitoring for whether Chinese trade coercion continues to backfire diplomatically.
insights.quote: what is striking today is how little such Chinese efforts have achieved so far, despite everything Trump has done to help Beijing’s cause.
